items.note: Two experiments assigned 139 business professionals and 319 working adults to low, moderate, or high collaboration with ChatGPT on an entrepreneurial challenge, with judge-, entrepreneur-, and AI-rated creativity (moderate best); a 188-person multiwave survey is a separate non-experimental study; random assignment and a no-AI arm are not stated in the abstract.

Two randomized experiments (flash fiction, song composition) compare creative work with and without generative AI by general versus domain-specific human capital; abstract gives no N or scoring details; AoM proceedings abstract and arXiv 2412.03963 are the same study.

Abstract not reachable (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, Europe PMC, ScienceDirect tried); search notes say AIGC-integrated versus conventional product-design ideation teaching with self-efficacy and possibly ideation novelty and variety outcomes; design and N need the full text.

AEA RCT registration only (no results): students write research proposals with AI allowed or banned, with expert-rated quality and innovativeness planned; planned 400 participants; likely drop at the next stage unless results exist.

Randomized experiment with 148 three-person teams (444 people) on a product-design task with AI during divergent search only, convergent selection only, the whole process, or never; human-rated creativity and semantic exploration measured; PsyArXiv preprint.

Six-week randomized instructional experiment with 120 visual-communication design students compares GenAI-integrated with traditional instruction, with blind expert ratings of creative performance; unit of randomization (students or classes) to check.

Quasi-experiment with two 12th-grade classes (61 students) that both used the ChatGPT-CIDI model, one individually and one in teams; the contrast is collaboration format, not AI assistance, and creativity showed no change in either group.

Counterbalanced within-subjects experiment: 61 design students randomly assigned to order of traditional tools versus AI image tools (Midjourney, DALL-E) for posters; blind expert ratings of the posters plus self-reported critical thinking.

Students in a digital content contest used generative AI (prompt-literacy group) or conventional digital tools (comparison group); creative problem-solving ability and curiosity compared, likely self-report scales; N and assignment not stated.

64 Korean undergraduates in a design-thinking Living Lab received emotional or neutral feedback from generative AI (one AI configuration versus another); quality of creative outputs plus self-reported creative self-efficacy and metacognition.
